rules/blueberries-need-strongly-acidic-s.b: Blueberries are acid-loving plants adapted to low-pH soils. At soil pH above about 5.5, iron is not available to the roots even when it is present in the soil, and the plant develops interveinal chlorosis (yellowing between the veins) on new growth. Lowering the pH with elemental sulfur makes iron available again; spraying the leaves with iron greens them only temporarily and leaves the soil, and so the plant's long-term health, uncorrected.

rules/cole-crop-set-out-too-early-can/.b: Cabbage, broccoli, cauliflower and their kin are biennials, so cold is their signal that a winter has passed and it is time to flower. A young plant that accumulates enough cold (a stretch of weather in the 40s F) is vernalized and switches from building leaves and a head to running up a flower stalk and setting seed. Set out before the weather has settled, a small transplant crosses that cold threshold before it has grown the leafy bulk a head needs, so it buttons (a tiny premature head) or bolts (runs to seed) and never heads properly.

Tassels shed pollen that must land on the silks of neighboring plants. In a single row much of the pollen blows out of the row, and each silk it misses is one missing kernel.

Restrictions are strictest for black currant (Ribes nigrum), the most susceptible type. A rust-immune cultivar breaks the cycle. It cannot host the rust, so it cannot pass it to a pine.

rules/dioecious-species-need-both-male-f.b: A dioecious species carries male and female flowers on separate plants. Some plants make only pollen, others only fruit. A lone plant, or a planting that is all one sex, sets no fruit at all, because there is no pollen to reach the female flowers. Fruit needs at least one male plant near the fruiting females. This is a different mechanism from the single-locus self-incompatibility of apple and pear. There a plant has both sexes and rejects only its own pollen; here whole plants are one sex. So it is a separate rule and does not widen that one.

rules/direct-sown-root-crop-left-unthinn.b: Root crops are sown as seed in place and germinate much denser than they can mature. Where the seedlings stand too close, their swelling roots run out of room and compete for space, water, and nutrients, so they stay undersized and are deformed, twisting and intertwining against their neighbors. Thinning the stand while the seedlings are young leaves each remaining root the room to develop. (This is distinct from FORKING, which the sources attribute to rocky or compacted soil and root-knot nematodes. So this rule claims small-and-intertwined roots and makes no claim about forking.)

Because the reservoir family may differ from the victim's, the same-family rotation intervals miss it.

rules/do-not-harvest-asparagus-all-first.b: Every spear is drawn from energy stored in the crown, and the ferns are what refill that store. The fern's photosynthesis is banked underground to produce the following year's spears. A young planting is still expanding its root storage system, so cutting its spears removes the shoots that would have become ferns, and excessive removal of spears weakens the plants. Restraint in the establishment years is what builds a crown strong enough to bear a full harvest for decades.

A host-free break cuts local carryover, but both are strong fliers that re-invade from a distance, so rotation is only partial and works best paired with fall sanitation (destroy spent vines).

rules/garlic-planted-autumn-not-spring-c.b: A garlic clove will not form a bulb until it has been vernalized, held for roughly six to eight weeks below about 40 °F. The bulb itself does not develop during that cold; it is only induced by it, and forms in spring as days lengthen and temperatures rise. Fall planting delivers the cold naturally over winter with the clove already rooted, so growth resumes early and a full bulb sizes up by early summer. It is the same biennial vernalization that prematurely bolts a spring-sown cool-season crop, but with the sign reversed. There the accumulated cold buttons the plant into an early flower and ruins it; here, in a crop sown in autumn to be harvested as a bulb, that same cold is the intended trigger.
rules/garlic-planted-autumn-not-spring-c.m: A person has checked it against its sources. If you skip this, it still grows, just less well. The planner suggests it.
rules/garlic-planted-autumn-not-spring-c.t: Garlic is planted in autumn, not spring

rules/grapes-fruit-new-shoots-that-grow-.b: Fruit forms only on shoots arising from last season's canes, so a vine left unpruned piles up old wood that no longer fruits while the crop crowds onto too many buds. Cutting back 80 to 90 percent of last year's growth concentrates the vine into a small number of well-placed, productive canes; prune too little and too many buds remain, so the vine over-produces small, poor fruit and becomes a tangled mass.
rules/grapes-fruit-new-shoots-that-grow-.m: A person has checked it against its sources. If you skip this, it still grows, just less well. The planner suggests it.
rules/grapes-fruit-new-shoots-that-grow-.t: Grapes fruit on new shoots that grow from last season's canes

rules/ground-gardener-has-observed-stand.b: Saturated soil has no air in it, so roots suffocate; and standing water lets Phytophthora release swimming zoospores, which need free water to reach a root or crown at all.
rules/ground-gardener-has-observed-stand.m: A person has checked it against its sources. If you skip this, you lose real yield. The planner warns you.
rules/ground-gardener-has-observed-stand.t: Ground the gardener has observed to stand water after rain is a site problem to fix before planting

rules/ground-that-has-carried-brassicas-.b: Plasmodiophora brassicae's resting spores germinate in wet soil below about pH 7.0, and alkaline soil with high calcium suppresses the infection; liming to 7.1 to 7.5 slowly reduces severity but is not reliable once an infestation is established.
rules/ground-that-has-carried-brassicas-.m: A person has checked it against its sources. If you skip this, it still grows, just less well. The planner suggests it.
rules/ground-that-has-carried-brassicas-.t: On ground that has carried brassicas within the rotation interval

rules/ground-that-just-carried-cereal-ry.b: Rye and sorghum roots and residue release allelochemicals (benzoxazinoids from rye, sorgoleone from sorghum) that persist in the surface soil for weeks after the cover is killed. A small seed sown into that layer has little reserve to push through the inhibition; a large seed or a transplant is already past the germination window.

rules/ground-that-just-carried-cereal-ry.t: Ground that just carried cereal rye or a sorghum cover crop is a poor seedbed for small seeds for a few weeks

rules/growing-vegetable-garden-needs-abo.b: Growing plants draw water out of the soil, and sun and air dry it from the top. What the rain does not put back, the soil loses until it is watered.
rules/growing-vegetable-garden-needs-abo.m: A person has checked it against its sources. If you skip this, it still grows, just less well. The planner suggests it.
rules/growing-vegetable-garden-needs-abo.t: Vegetables need about an inch of water a week

rules/hardiness-zone-correct-variable-pe.b: Zones encode average annual minimum winter temperature, which governs whether a woody perennial survives to spring. It is the wrong quantity for an annual, which never sees winter. A zone that is too warm is a second, different mechanism. Mild winters do not kill a perennial; they fail to chill it. Deciduous fruit crops need a winter dormancy period to break bud and set fruit, so in a zone milder than a plant is adapted to it may survive and never crop. Only the cold end is enforced, because only winter survival follows from what a zone measures; the warm end gets advice and is never refused. That warm limit is a property of the cultivar, and that limits what this rule can do. Chill requirement is published per variety and varies enormously within a species, so a species-level ceiling says "the modeled range does not reach your zone", never "no plant of this kind will crop for you". So above its range the planner still offers the plant, with advice to choose a cultivar rated for your zone.
rules/hardiness-zone-correct-variable-pe.m: A person has checked it against its sources. If you skip this, it still grows, just less well. The planner suggests it.
rules/hardiness-zone-correct-variable-pe.t: Hardiness zone is the correct variable for perennials

rules/hardy-half-hardy-crops-stand-light.b: A hardy or half-hardy crop's tissue survives the ice of a light freeze down to about 28 °F (-2 °C), so its season ends at the first night that cold, which comes after the first 32 °F frost, and later still where winters are mild.

rules/hardy-half-hardy-crops-stand-light.t: Hardy crops can go in later, counted back from the freeze they can't stand

rules/heat-bolters-that-tolerate-part-su.b: Leaf temperature. Shade from a taller crop lowers the leaf and soil temperature of the greens beneath it, and high summer temperature is the trigger that sends these species to seed and turns them bitter.

rules/hot-weather-water-early-morning-be.b: Less water evaporates from the soil in the cool of the morning than in the heat of the day, so more of what you give soaks in and reaches the roots.

rules/how-often-water-weather-question-s.b: How fast ground dries is set by rainfall, temperature, wind and humidity in your own bed, day by day. Monthly normals describe a usual month and a forecast a coming week, and neither sees your soil, so an interval computed from them is a guess wearing a schedule's clothes.

rules/insect-pollinated-crop-depends-ins.b: A monoecious cucurbit bears pollen and ovules in separate flowers, so fertilization requires a vector to carry pollen between them. Neither wind nor self-fertility applies. Ovules that are not fertilized do not develop, and the fruit aborts or forms misshapen.
rules/insect-pollinated-crop-depends-ins.m: A person has checked it against its sources. If you skip this, it still grows, just less well. The planner suggests it.
rules/insect-pollinated-crop-depends-ins.t: An insect-pollinated crop depends on an insect to move pollen between its flowers

rules/insectary-plants-near-fruiting-cro.b: The flowers supply nectar and pollen that adult predators and parasitoids feed on, so a patch of them near a fruiting crop keeps those beneficial insects fed and close by to work the crop. The effect is real but not guaranteed. An insectary patch does not always suppress pests.
rules/insectary-plants-near-fruiting-cro.m: A person has checked it against its sources. If you skip this, it still grows, just less well. The planner suggests it.
rules/insectary-plants-near-fruiting-cro.t: Insectary plants near fruiting crops increase pollinator and predator visitation.

rules/large-ragged-holes-chewed-cabbage-.b: The adult is a white butterfly with black spots on its forewings that lays its eggs on cole crops. The caterpillars grow to about an inch, velvety green with faint yellow stripes, and the larger ones chew large, ragged holes in the leaves, leaving the big veins.

rules/late-blight-comes-back-from-last-y.b: Phytophthora infestans needs living tissue to overwinter. Infected tubers left in the ground, in a compost heap that does not freeze, or in a cull pile survive and sprout as volunteers that carry the blight into the new season; tomatoes do not carry it, because frost kills the whole plant and the seed is clean.

rules/late-season-when-squash-plants-los.b: Sun scald. As a squash plant ages its leaves die back and leave the fruit uncovered, and strong summer sun burns the exposed rind. Corn standing in the same bed casts shade over that fruit.
rules/late-season-when-squash-plants-los.m: A person has checked it against its sources. If you skip this, it still grows, just less well. The planner suggests it.

rules/layer-organic-mulch-over-soil-cuts.b: Mulch covers and shades the soil, so less of its water evaporates from the surface and the moisture below stays more even.

rules/layer-organic-mulch-over-soil-cuts.t: Mulch can cut a bed's watering by around half.

rules/legume-fixes-atmospheric-nitrogen-.b: Nitrogen fixation happens in root nodules formed by Rhizobium or Bradyrhizobium bacteria specific to each legume group. On ground that has not grown that legume group before (a new bed, a soil-less mix, a long gap in the rotation, a fumigated or strongly acid soil), the matching strain can be absent or sparse, so nodulation and fixation are reduced until a population builds.

rules/legume-fixes-atmospheric-nitrogen-.t: Beans, peas and other legumes only fix nitrogen with the right soil bacteria

rules/legume-green-manure-raises-availab.b: A legume fixes atmospheric nitrogen into its tissue as it grows. When the crop is killed and its residue decomposes, soil microbes mineralize that organic nitrogen, converting a form plants can't use into one they can, and release it for the next crop. How much depends on how well the legume grew, and it is lower on sandy soils.
rules/legume-green-manure-raises-availab.m: A person has checked it against its sources. If you skip this, it still grows, just less well. The planner suggests it.
rules/legume-green-manure-raises-availab.t: Legume green manure raises available N for the subsequent crop.

rules/lemon-balm-self-sows-freely-left-f.b: The spread is chiefly by self-sown seed. A plant left to flower sets abundant seed that drops and germinates in place, so it recurs and expands from year to year. Removing the flowering stalks before seed sets breaks that cycle. Its spread is by seed. It does not travel by the running underground stems that carry its relative mint, though a soil-grown plant can also creep somewhat at its edges.

rules/lemon-balm-self-sows-freely-left-f.t: Lemon balm self-sows freely and, left to flower and set seed unchecked, spreads and can take over a bed

rules/lettuce-spinach-sowing-that-comes-.b: Long days and several days in a row above about 24 °C (75 °F) switch lettuce and spinach from making leaves to making a flower stalk, which turns the leaves bitter and ends the harvest.

rules/lightweight-fabric-floating-row-co.b: Floating row cover is a gauze-like spun sheet laid loosely over the crop and sealed at its edges to the soil, and it stops damage by physical exclusion (the adult insect cannot reach the plant to feed or lay eggs), so the barrier must be continuous from planting, before the pests arrive, with its edges buried against a walking insect; because the same closed barrier also shuts out the bee, a crop whose fruit depends on insect pollination has to be uncovered once its flowers open.

rules/limed-ground-wrong-ground-next-pot.b: Common scab (Streptomyces scabies) infects young tubers through the lenticels and is favored as soil goes less acid; at about pH 5.2 and below it is largely suppressed. Lime raises pH and its effect lasts years, so ground limed for a crop that wants sweet soil carries a scab-prone pH into the seasons that follow.

rules/living-mulch-suppresses-weeds-cons.b: A living cover keeps a leaf canopy over the ground. It intercepts light at the soil surface, so weed seedlings are shaded out before they establish, and it slows surface evaporation, so the soil holds more water. In a Three Sisters planting this is the squash's role. Its broad leaves shade the bed.

rules/lower-tomato-leaves-that-yellow-af.b: Early blight and Septoria leaf spot are fungal diseases that begin on the lower foliage in wet weather as deep brown or blackish spots, followed by yellowing or browning of the leaves. Early blight has target-like rings, and Septoria has whitish centers and dark borders. Separately, tomato leaves can yellow from a lack of nitrogen, which is common in containers because frequent watering and low soil fertility leave little of it.

Above an acid-requiring plant's range the same curve runs the other way. Iron becomes unavailable and the plant goes chlorotic.

rules/mint-spreads-aggressively-undergro.b: Rhizomatous, and stoloniferous, spread. Mint's horizontal underground stems (rhizomes) and its surface runners root at their nodes and send up new shoots, so an unconfined plant expands outward from the crown each season and reappears wherever a node reaches soil. This vegetative creep is why a loose planting takes over a bed, and why the control is a physical soil barrier. Spacing does not contain it.

rules/month-whose-normal-days-run-above-.t: In the hottest months, expect to water every day or every other day.

Field mice rarely touch daffodils even where they readily eat tulips and crocus, so a ring of narcissus tends to be left alone. It works by avoidance. It discourages feeding on the bulbs but is no barrier and no guarantee against every rodent.

rules/nasturtiums-bloom-best-lean-poor-a.b: Rich soil and abundant nitrogen bias the plant toward vegetative leaf growth over flowering; lean, low-fertility soil shifts the same balance back toward bloom. It is the foliage-over-flower tradeoff that heavy feeding produces in many plants, here spending the plant on leaves at the cost of the flowers it was grown for.

rules/nasturtiums-bloom-best-lean-poor-a.t: Nasturtiums bloom best in lean, poor-to-average, well-drained soil in full sun

rules/new-june-bearing-strawberry-planti.b: A first-year plant that ripens fruit spends on berries the resources that would otherwise build the root system, leaf canopy and runners (daughter plants) that make up next year's bed; letting the flowers develop into berries reduces plant growth, runner production and the size of next year's crop, while removing them directs the plant's resources into a large root system and a healthy plant. June-bearers crop once a year, so the whole first season is given to establishment; everbearing and day-neutral types keep flowering, so only the establishment window is sacrificed and later flowers are allowed to fruit.

rules/night-whose-forecast-low-36-f-2/.t: Frost can form on a night the forecast low is a few degrees above freezing.

rules/onion-cultivar-group-match-site-la.b: Bulbing fires when daylength crosses a cultivar's critical threshold (short ~10-12h, intermediate ~12-14h, long ~14-16h). A short-day cultivar grown too far from the equator crosses its low threshold early and bulbs prematurely on small plants, so bulbs stay small. A long-day cultivar grown too close to it never reaches its high threshold and fails to bulb. Changeover is around the 35th-38th parallel, north or south.

rules/onion-cultivar-group-match-site-la.t: Onion cultivar group must match site latitude.

rules/onions-garlic-lifted-storage-cured.b: At harvest the bulb's neck and outer scales are still moist living tissue and the neck is an open channel into the bulb, so curing in warm moving air dries the neck shut and the outer scales to a papery protective skin, removing the wet tissue that storage rots colonise and sealing the neck they enter by; an uncured bulb goes into storage with a moist open neck and soft scales, and decays.
rules/onions-garlic-lifted-storage-cured.m: A person has checked it against its sources. If you skip this, it still grows, just less well. The planner suggests it.
rules/onions-garlic-lifted-storage-cured.t: Cure onions and garlic before you store them

rules/over-feeding-tomato-nitrogen-grows.b: High available nitrogen biases the plant toward vegetative growth. Abundant nitrogen keeps it building leaves and stems, and that leaf-and-stem growth takes priority over the switch into flowering, so flower initiation is delayed and fewer flowers form. The visible result is lush dark foliage with reduced and later fruit set, with the growth spent on leaves and stems.
rules/over-feeding-tomato-nitrogen-grows.m: A person has checked it against its sources. If you skip this, it still grows, just less well. The planner suggests it.
rules/over-feeding-tomato-nitrogen-grows.t: Over-feeding a tomato with nitrogen grows a tall, dark-green, leafy plant that flowers late and sets little fruit

rules/pepper-fruit-set-suffers-when-nigh.b: Warm nights above ~21 °C (70 °F) weaken pepper growth and, together with hot days, leave flowers poorly pollinated so they drop before setting fruit. Pepper carries a second heat driver this night threshold does not see. Daytime highs above ~34 °C (93 °F) also abort the flowers, so this rule catches only the night half of a two-sided problem.

rules/pepper-fruit-set-suffers-when-nigh.t: Pepper fruit set suffers when night temperatures stay above ~21 °C

rules/perennial-members-not-be-sited-gro.t: Perennial members must not be sited in ground that is annually turned or rotated.

rules/planted-bed-keeps-plant-within-arm.b: You can comfortably reach about 2 feet (0.6 m) into a bed. Soil farther than that from a path or edge can only be tended by stepping on it, which packs it down. So a bed worked from its edges and wider than about 4 feet (1.2 m) is laid out as planting strips no wider than 4 feet, with paths about 20 inches (0.5 m) between them. A field is worked from rows you walk, about 2.5 feet (0.75 m) apart. Raised beds, in-ground beds and containers are worked from their edges; a field is walked.
rules/planted-bed-keeps-plant-within-arm.m: A person has checked it against its sources. If you skip this, it still grows, just less well. The planner suggests it.
rules/planted-bed-keeps-plant-within-arm.t: A planted bed keeps every plant within arm's reach of a path, edge, or walkable row.

rules/plants-over-120cm-mature-height-be.b: Solar geometry. Shadow falls outside the bed, clear of shorter neighbors.
rules/plants-over-120cm-mature-height-be.m: It is settled without a trial. If you skip this, you lose real yield. The planner warns you.
rules/plants-over-120cm-mature-height-be.t: Plants over 120cm mature height belong on the north side of a bed.

rules/potato-tubers-that-catch-light-whi.b: Tuber tissue exposed to light produces chlorophyll and, in that same tissue, synthesises the toxic glycoalkaloids solanine and chaconine, so soil mounded over the developing tubers keeps light off them and prevents both the greening and the toxin from forming.
rules/potato-tubers-that-catch-light-whi.m: A person has checked it against its sources. This one is about eating safely, not how the plant grows. The planner suggests it.
rules/potato-tubers-that-catch-light-whi.t: Potato tubers that catch light while growing

rules/potatoes-grown-from-certified-seed.b: Potato is propagated vegetatively (the crop grows from a piece of tuber), so any virus or disease in the seed tuber is passed straight to the new plants and can remain in the soil for years; certified seed is inspected, disease-free stock, which is why saving one's own tubers or planting grocery potatoes risks introducing disease. Each planted piece must carry an eye, the bud the new shoot grows from. A freshly cut piece exposes moist flesh that storage and soil rots colonise; holding the cut pieces a few days until the surface dries and forms a corky protective layer (suberises) seals that wound before planting. Grocery tubers may additionally be treated with a sprout inhibitor, so they are slow to grow.
rules/potatoes-grown-from-certified-seed.m: A person has checked it against its sources. If you skip this, it still grows, just less well. The planner suggests it.
rules/potatoes-grown-from-certified-seed.t: Potatoes are grown from certified seed potatoes

rules/prism-offset-from-nearby-station-a.b: PRISM models orography, temperature inversions, slope aspect, and coastal proximity at 800m. It provides monthly mean/min/max temperature. It does not provide frost exceedance probabilities; those exist only at stations. Combining them is an inference.
rules/prism-offset-from-nearby-station-a.m: A person has checked it against its sources. If you skip this, it still grows, just less well. The planner suggests it.
rules/prism-offset-from-nearby-station-a.t: Adjusting a nearby station's frost date assumes average night lows track frost dates

rules/raspberry-blackberry-canes-biennia.b: Each cane lives two years while the crown persists. A vegetative primocane in year one becomes the fruiting floricane in year two, and a floricane dies after fruiting, and it will not fruit again or survive another winter. Next year's fruiting wood is therefore this year's primocanes, so removing them removes the crop. The spent floricanes are cut at ground level because dead stubs left standing can harbor canker-causing fungi.
rules/raspberry-blackberry-canes-biennia.m: A person has checked it against its sources. If you skip this, it still grows, just less well. The planner suggests it.
rules/raspberry-blackberry-canes-biennia.t: Raspberry and blackberry canes are biennial

rules/rhubarb-leaf-blades-poisonous-neve.b: The leaf blades hold a toxic concentration of oxalic acid (and, per NDSU, anthraquinone glycosides), which the edible petioles carry only in trace amounts. Oxalic acid binds calcium and can damage kidney function; eating the blades causes cramping, nausea and, in quantity, can be fatal. The stalks are safe because the toxins concentrate in the leaf.
rules/rhubarb-leaf-blades-poisonous-neve.m: A person has checked it against its sources. This one is about eating safely, not how the plant grows. The planner suggests it.
rules/rhubarb-leaf-blades-poisonous-neve.t: Rhubarb leaf blades are poisonous and must never be eaten

rules/rosemary-sage-thyme-oregano-medite.b: These species are adapted to dry-climate Mediterranean conditions, with gritty, fast-draining soils and low summer water. In wet or heavy, poorly drained soil the root zone stays waterlogged, starving the roots of oxygen and rotting them; excess water and rich fertility compound the rot risk and, in these aromatic herbs, thin the essential oils that carry the flavor.
rules/rosemary-sage-thyme-oregano-medite.m: A person has checked it against its sources. If you skip this, it still grows, just less well. The planner suggests it.
rules/rosemary-sage-thyme-oregano-medite.t: Rosemary, sage, thyme and oregano like full sun, sharp drainage and lean soil

rules/row-cover-low-tunnel-cold-frame-le.b: Soil warmed by the sun by day is the heat source at night; a covering low to the ground traps that heat around the plants on calm, clear nights, keeping them a few degrees above the open air through the light frosts at each end of the season.
rules/row-cover-low-tunnel-cold-frame-le.m: A person has checked it against its sources. If you skip this, it still grows, just less well. The planner suggests it.
rules/row-cover-low-tunnel-cold-frame-le.t: A cover buys cool-season crops a week or two at the ends of the season.

rules/seed-comes-up-from-warmth-soil-not.b: Germination is driven by temperature-dependent enzymes that mobilise the seed's stored reserves, so in soil below the species' range those enzymes work too slowly for the seedling to emerge before soil fungi rot the water-swollen seed, and in soil above the range that same enzyme machinery is suppressed. That is why the soil's own temperature is the reliable signal, and the day of the year is not.
rules/seed-comes-up-from-warmth-soil-not.m: A person has checked it against its sources. If you skip this, it still grows, just less well. The planner suggests it.
rules/seed-comes-up-from-warmth-soil-not.t: A seed comes up from the warmth of the soil, not from a date on the calendar

rules/seedling-raised-indoors-set-out-gr.b: Indoor-raised seedlings grow soft, with a thin cuticle and waxy layer, unlignified stems, and high tissue water, because the light, wind, and temperature swings that toughen a plant are absent indoors. Exposed abruptly to direct sun the thin leaves scald, in wind the soft stems break or desiccate, and the whole plant stalls from the shock. Hardening off (a week or two of increasing daily outdoor exposure) thickens the cuticle and waxy layers, develops lignin in the cell walls, builds carbohydrate reserves, and lowers freeze-prone cell water, so the plant can take the move.
rules/seedling-raised-indoors-set-out-gr.m: A person has checked it against its sources. If you skip this, it still grows, just less well. The planner suggests it.
rules/seedling-raised-indoors-set-out-gr.t: A seedling raised indoors is set out gradually, not all at once

rules/seedlings-raised-cool-wet-reused-g.b: Damping-off is caused by soil-borne fungi (chiefly Rhizoctonia and Fusarium species and the water mold Pythium) that infect the germinating seed or the young stem at the soil surface, rotting it so the seedling fails to emerge or topples at the base. The pathogens thrive in cool, wet medium with poor drainage, and anything that slows the seedling's own growth (low light, overwatering, cool soil, high fertilizer salts) widens the window in which they attack.
rules/seedlings-raised-cool-wet-reused-g.m: A person has checked it against its sources. If you skip this, it still grows, just less well. The planner suggests it.
rules/seedlings-raised-cool-wet-reused-g.t: Seedlings raised in cool, wet, or reused growing medium can collapse from damping-off

rules/self-incompatible-pome-fruit-s-pol.b: Cross-pollination only works while both cultivars' flowers are open together, so their bloom periods must overlap: early with mid, or mid with late. Early and late can miss each other entirely. A normal cultivar makes viable pollen; a triploid apple, with three sets of chromosomes instead of two, makes little or none and cannot fertilize a partner even though it needs one itself. Two plants of a single variety, including a colored sport of it, are genetically identical, so they reject each other's pollen exactly as a lone tree does.
rules/self-incompatible-pome-fruit-s-pol.m: A person has checked it against its sources. If you skip this, it still grows, just less well. The planner suggests it.
rules/self-incompatible-pome-fruit-s-pol.t: A self-incompatible pome fruit's pollen partner has to bloom at the same time and make viable pollen

rules/self-incompatible-species-require-.b: Many fruit trees carry self-incompatibility alleles at a single locus. When a pollen grain shares an allele with the pistil it lands on, the pistil rejects it and no seed sets. A plant's own pollen always shares its alleles, so it cannot fertilize itself. Neither can a second tree of the identical variety, which is genetically the same. Fertilization needs pollen from a genetically distinct plant.
rules/self-incompatible-species-require-.m: A person has checked it against its sources. If you skip this, you lose real yield. The planner warns you.
rules/self-incompatible-species-require-.t: Some plants can't fruit from their own pollen

rules/small-soft-pear-shaped-insects-clu.b: Aphids feed on plant sap, injecting saliva into the host as they feed. Severe feeding twists and curls the leaves, yellows the foliage, stunts or kills shoots and slows growth. They secrete a sticky, sugary honeydew that can let sooty mold grow on the leaves, though the honeydew itself does not harm the plant.
rules/small-soft-pear-shaped-insects-clu.m: A person has checked it against its sources. If you skip this, it still grows, just less well. The planner suggests it.
rules/small-soft-pear-shaped-insects-clu.t: Small, soft, pear-shaped insects clustered on a plant, with twisted and curled leaves, are aphids

rules/some-seed-will-not-germinate-strai.b: A hard, water-impermeable seed coat holds the seed dormant by blocking imbibition, so nicking, abrading, or soaking the coat is what lets water reach the embryo; a seed with physiological dormancy stays shut until a period of cold, moist chilling lets its germination-inhibiting hormones dissipate. So each treatment takes its own span of time, and starting it late leaves the seed still dormant at sowing.
rules/some-seed-will-not-germinate-strai.m: A person has checked it against its sources. If you skip this, it still grows, just less well. The planner suggests it.
rules/some-seed-will-not-germinate-strai.t: Some seed will not germinate straight from the packet

rules/specialist-pest-pathogen-finds-bui.b: Resource concentration. A specialist locates and holds its host more efficiently at higher host density and continuity, so an unbroken run of one family across adjacent beds is an easier target than the same family separated by a non-host (associational resistance).
rules/specialist-pest-pathogen-finds-bui.m: A person has checked it against its sources. If you skip this, it still grows, just less well. The planner suggests it.
rules/specialist-pest-pathogen-finds-bui.t: Pests of one plant family spread more easily through a solid block of it

rules/species-reach-maturity-within-site.b: The season's accumulated growing degree days (a running total of its warmth) against the total the crop needs to mature, or the crop's days to maturity against the number of frost-free days.
rules/species-reach-maturity-within-site.m: A person has checked it against its sources. If you skip this, the planting fails. The planner won’t allow it.
rules/species-reach-maturity-within-site.t: Don't plant a crop that can't mature before your frost-free season ends

rules/squash-pumpkin-runner-that-suddenl.b: The adult is a day-flying moth that lays its eggs singly at the base of the plant, on leaf stalks and on vines. The larvae tunnel into the stem to feed, and their feeding destroys the vine's vascular tissue, stopping water and nutrient movement, and that is the sudden wilt. As they feed they push frass out of holes in the side of the stem.
rules/squash-pumpkin-runner-that-suddenl.m: A person has checked it against its sources. If you skip this, it still grows, just less well. The planner suggests it.
rules/squash-pumpkin-runner-that-suddenl.t: Sudden wilt with sawdust at stem holes means a squash vine borer

rules/stone-fruit-shares-brown-rot-overw.b: Monilinia fructicola overwinters in mummified fruit left on the tree or the ground and in twig cankers; at bloom its spores blow and splash to blossoms, and infected fruit sheds spores that spread to other fruit on the same tree and to neighboring trees, wild Prunus included.
rules/stone-fruit-shares-brown-rot-overw.m: A person has checked it against its sources. If you skip this, it still grows, just less well. The planner suggests it.
rules/stone-fruit-shares-brown-rot-overw.t: Every stone fruit shares brown rot, and it overwinters on the tree

rules/succession-sowing-intervals-about-.b: Sowing the same crop in batches about two weeks apart staggers when each batch matures, so the harvest arrives as a continual succession, with no single glut. It pays off only for short-DTM crops, whose quick turnaround lets several sowings ripen within a single season.
rules/succession-sowing-intervals-about-.m: A person has checked it against its sources. If you skip this, it still grows, just less well. The planner suggests it.
rules/succession-sowing-intervals-about-.t: Succession sowing at intervals of about two weeks extends harvest for short-DTM crops.

rules/sun-requiring-species-not-sit-comp.b: Photosynthesis. Compute shadow polygons from latitude, date, and mature height.
rules/sun-requiring-species-not-sit-comp.m: It is settled without a trial. If you skip this, you lose real yield. The planner warns you.
rules/sun-requiring-species-not-sit-comp.t: Sun-requiring species must not sit in the computed shadow of a taller neighbor.

rules/sunflower-residue-suppresses-germi.b: Sunflower tissue and roots release allelochemicals that persist in the soil and inhibit the germination and early growth of sensitive plants. Small-seeded, direct-sown neighbors are the ones at risk. A small seed has little reserve to push through the inhibition, whereas a transplant is already past the germination window and largely escapes.

rules/sunflower-residue-suppresses-germi.t: Sunflower residue suppresses germination of some small-seeded species.

rules/tender-species-not-be-scheduled-be.t: Don't sow or set out tender crops before your last frost date

rules/three-more-seasons-logged-frost-ou.b: Garden-scale microclimate (south wall, frost pocket, raised-bed drainage, urban heat island) lives below 800m resolution and below 80m. No gridded product resolves it. The season log is a direct measurement on the exact ground in question.
rules/three-more-seasons-logged-frost-ou.m: A person has checked it against its sources. If you skip this, it still grows, just less well. The planner suggests it.
rules/three-more-seasons-logged-frost-ou.t: Your own frost records from 3+ seasons outrank any climate model for your plot

rules/tomato-eggplant-set-little-fruit-w.b: Low temperatures cut the pollen's viability and slow the growth of the pollen tube, so the flowers drop without setting fruit.
rules/tomato-eggplant-set-little-fruit-w.m: A person has checked it against its sources. If you skip this, you lose real yield. The planner warns you.
rules/tomato-eggplant-set-little-fruit-w.t: Tomatoes, peppers and eggplant set little fruit while the nights stay cool.

rules/tomato-fruit-set-fails-when-night-.b: Sustained high day (>29-32 °C / 85-90 °F) and night (>21 °C / 70 °F) temperatures make pollen non-viable ("tacky") and impair its release; flowers go unfertilized within their ~50-hour window and abscise.

rules/tomato-fruit-set-fails-when-night-.t: Tomato fruit set fails when night temperatures persistently exceed ~21 °C

rules/tomato-transplant-goes-into-ground.b: A tomato's stem forms roots along whatever length of it is buried in moist soil. Setting the plant deep therefore converts stem into root, and the plant ends up with a larger root system than the one that came out of the pot.
rules/tomato-transplant-goes-into-ground.m: A person has checked it against its sources. If you skip this, it still grows, just less well. The planner suggests it.
rules/tomato-transplant-goes-into-ground.t: A tomato transplant goes into the ground deeper than it grew in its pot, buried up to its first leaves

rules/tree-fruits-differ-whether-lone-tr.b: A self-unfruitful tree will not set a normal crop from its own pollen or the pollen of another tree of the same cultivar; it needs pollen from a genetically different, compatible cultivar, carried by bees while both trees are in bloom. That is why the partner must be a different cultivar, must bloom at the same time, and must stand within a bee's working range. It is also why a self-fruitful species like peach or sour cherry, whose own pollen sets fruit, bears alone.
rules/tree-fruits-differ-whether-lone-tr.m: A person has checked it against its sources. If you skip this, it still grows, just less well. The planner suggests it.
rules/tree-fruits-differ-whether-lone-tr.t: Tree fruits differ in whether a lone tree can set a crop

rules/tree-shrub-plant-team-s-ground-dri.b: A tree's root zone expands for a decade and extends well past the canopy edge.
rules/tree-shrub-plant-team-s-ground-dri.m: A person has checked it against its sources. If you skip this, it still grows, just less well. The planner suggests it.
rules/tree-shrub-plant-team-s-ground-dri.t: A tree or shrub plant team's ground is its drip-line ring, not a bed

rules/two-kinds-corn-tasseling-together-.b: Corn is wind-pollinated and the pollen parent sets the kernel's endosperm (xenia), so a sweet-corn ear fertilized by a starchy type stores starch, and a supersweet ear fertilized by any other type reverts to the toughness of field corn. Standard, sugary-enhanced and synergistic sweet corns need no isolation from each other.
rules/two-kinds-corn-tasseling-together-.m: A person has checked it against its sources. If you skip this, you lose real yield. The planner warns you.
rules/two-kinds-corn-tasseling-together-.t: Two kinds of corn tasseling together spoil each other's kernels

rules/very-tender-crops-go-out-about-two.b: Chilling. A very tender crop is hurt by cool weather as well as by frost: it needs daytime temperatures above 60 °F, and a week of days below 55 °F can stunt it. Setting it out about two weeks after the average last frost gives the days time to warm.
rules/very-tender-crops-go-out-about-two.m: A person has checked it against its sources. If you skip this, it still grows, just less well. The planner suggests it.
rules/very-tender-crops-go-out-about-two.t: Very tender crops go out about two weeks after the average last spring frost

rules/vine-assigned-living-support-be-so.b: Load. A bean vine on an immature, poorly-anchored stalk pulls it over; extension guides key the delay to the support's height (corn ~6 in) as a proxy for it being rooted enough to bear the climbing load.

rules/vine-assigned-living-support-be-so.t: A vine assigned to a living support must be sown after the support is established, when corn is ~6 in

rules/vining-cucurbits-beds-under-about-.b: Vining squash and pumpkins run along the ground and take up a lot of space: the guides space large-vined ones in rows 6 to 8 feet (1.8 to 2.4 m) apart, so a narrower bed leaves them nowhere to go but out.

rules/vining-cucurbits-beds-under-about-.t: Vining cucurbits in beds under about 2 m (6 to 8 ft) escape the bed.

rules/warm-season-bean-germinates-from-w.b: Warm-season legumes take up water fast at sowing (imbibition), and in cold soil that first rush of cold water injures the seed tissue before the seedling can establish (imbibitional chilling), so the seed rots or comes up damaged. Soil below about 15 °C (60 °F) at sowing depth is where this bites, and the frost-free date can arrive weeks before the soil is that warm.
rules/warm-season-bean-germinates-from-w.m: A person has checked it against its sources. If you skip this, it still grows, just less well. The planner suggests it.
rules/warm-season-bean-germinates-from-w.t: A warm-season bean germinates from warm soil, whatever the calendar says

rules/water-soil-not-leaves-film-water-l.b: A spore landing on a leaf needs liquid water on that surface to germinate and enter it. Water delivered to the soil never puts a film there; water thrown over the plant does, and the longer it lasts the more of the spores already present can use it.
rules/water-soil-not-leaves-film-water-l.m: A person has checked it against its sources. If you skip this, it still grows, just less well. The planner suggests it.
rules/water-soil-not-leaves-film-water-l.t: Water the soil, not the leaves

rules/where-frost-does-not-end-season-cr.b: A crop grows and makes its harvest within a band of warmth: in months colder than its band it grows too slowly to finish, and in months hotter than it a cool-season crop bolts and turns bitter while a warm-season crop drops its flowers.
rules/where-frost-does-not-end-season-cr.m: A person has checked it against its sources. If you skip this, you lose real yield. The planner suggests it.
rules/where-frost-does-not-end-season-cr.t: Where frost is rare, sow so the crop grows through months that suit it.

rules/where-frost-rare-year-has-dry-seas.b: A new tree's roots have not yet reached deeper moisture, so it settles in on steady rain or watering, and planting into the rains gives it that water.
rules/where-frost-rare-year-has-dry-seas.m: A person has checked it against its sources. If you skip this, it still grows, just less well. The planner suggests it.
rules/where-frost-rare-year-has-dry-seas.t: Where frost is rare, plant a young fruit tree as the rains begin.

rules/where-frost-sets-season-crop-reach.b: A crop grows at the pace its days to maturity assume only in months at least as warm as the low end of its band, and in cooler months it grows too slowly to finish, so a frost-free season of cool months can end before the crop is ready.
rules/where-frost-sets-season-crop-reach.m: A person has yet to check it against a source. If you skip this, you lose real yield. The planner suggests it.

rules/where-no-weather-station-model-ans.b: Each logged frost is a direct observation of when frost reached that ground. With no station or model to correct, the middle of those observations is the plot's only frost estimate, and because frost dates swing from year to year, a middle taken from a few seasons is rough.
rules/where-no-weather-station-model-ans.m: A person has checked it against its sources. If you skip this, it still grows, just less well. The planner suggests it.
rules/where-no-weather-station-model-ans.t: Where no station or model reaches, 3+ seasons of your own frosts give rough dates

rules/white-powdery-spots-squash-cucumbe.b: The fungus (mainly Podosphaera xanthii) grows on the leaf surface; the spores formed in each spot are carried by the wind to other leaves, and under favorable conditions it spreads until it covers most of the foliage. A plant that loses most of its leaf area to it is weakened, and its fruit ripens prematurely. It takes hold most readily on densely planted vines, plants crowded by weeds, plants in shade and over-fertilized plants.
rules/white-powdery-spots-squash-cucumbe.m: A person has checked it against its sources. If you skip this, it still grows, just less well. The planner suggests it.
rules/white-powdery-spots-squash-cucumbe.t: White powdery spots on squash, cucumber, melon or pumpkin leaves are powdery mildew

rules/winter-cover-crop-sown-autumn-set-.b: The plants need time to germinate and grow before the first hard frost and short days force them into dormancy; sown too late, a cover crop neither covers the soil through winter nor survives to grow again in spring. Sown too early, crimson clover can go to seed in the fall and not regrow until the soil warms. Cereal rye tolerates the latest sowing of the three.
rules/winter-cover-crop-sown-autumn-set-.m: A person has checked it against its sources. If you skip this, it still grows, just less well. The planner suggests it.
rules/winter-cover-crop-sown-autumn-set-.t: A winter cover crop is sown in autumn a set time before the first fall frost

rules/young-apple-stone-fruit-tree-plant.b: Apple leaves behind a soil complex of fungi and oomycetes (Rhizoctonia, Ilyonectria, Phytophthora, Pythium) together with the lesion nematode Pratylenchus penetrans; the stone fruits leave the genus-wide version, Prunus replant disease, and in peach the ring nematode with the bacterial- canker organism drives its severe named form, Peach Tree Short Life. Either way a young tree of the same kind meets that loaded soil with a root system too small to outgrow it.
rules/young-apple-stone-fruit-tree-plant.m: A person has checked it against its sources. If you skip this, it still grows, just less well. The planner suggests it.
rules/young-apple-stone-fruit-tree-plant.t: A young apple or stone-fruit tree planted where an old one of its kind stood tends to sulk

rules/young-transplant-can-be-cut-off-so.b: Cutworms are the soil-dwelling caterpillars of several night-flying moths. They feed after dark, curling the body around a seedling's stem and chewing through it at or just above the soil surface, which topples the whole plant. A young transplant is vulnerable because its stem is small and tender; as the plant grows the stem thickens past what a cutworm can encircle and cut, so the risk is an early-season one. A collar of cardboard, stiff paper, or foil, set around the stem and pushed into the soil, is a physical barrier the cutworm can neither climb over nor tunnel under to reach the stem.
rules/young-transplant-can-be-cut-off-so.m: A person has checked it against its sources. If you skip this, it still grows, just less well. The planner suggests it.
rules/young-transplant-can-be-cut-off-so.t: A young transplant can be cut off at the soil line overnight by a cutworm
